description: We’re AstroCortex, a team from Lima, Peru. Our viewer pairs real SPHEREx images you can replay across dates with measurements of each target’s light. We also trained an experimental AI model on known stars and brown dwarfs to suggest objects for closer review. We built AstroCortex so students and curious observers can use real telescope data to investigate what moved or changed in brightness.
summary:
AstroCortex is a public web tool that shows how a small patch of sky changes over time in real NASA SPHEREx infrared images, and helps people find the Sun’s coldest neighbors: T and Y brown dwarfs. Users pick an object or a position, watch dated SPHEREx frames without interpolation, and ask a guided assistant what to look for, in simple or expert mode, in English and Spanish.

Behind it, we trained a machine-learning model on known stars and brown dwarfs. It uses infrared colors (WISE, 2MASS) and motion across the sky to suggest objects worth investigating. We validated it by sky region, kept a reserved region sealed, and had a second AI audit every step. In development data it separates T/Y dwarfs from other objects with 94% precision, and it classified four newly published T dwarfs correctly.

It matters because follow-up telescope time is scarce, and because real mission data should be within everyone’s reach.
details:
What it does and how it works. AstroCortex is a public web viewer for real NASA SPHEREx infrared images. You search by name or coordinates, choose a target such as the cold brown dwarf WISE 0855, and compare dated frames of the same field in a flipbook, with no interpolation. Spectrum and light-curve views and a step-by-step guide explain what you are seeing. Alongside the viewer, a machine-learning model trained on known stars and brown dwarfs uses infrared colors and motion across the sky to suggest objects worth investigating.

Benefits and impact. Researchers get a ranked shortlist instead of a blind search, so scarce follow-up telescope time goes to likelier targets. Students and the public get real mission data explained in plain language. The pipeline is reproducible, so new SPHEREx releases can be added.

Tools. Data: SPHEREx Level-2 images (NASA/IPAC IRSA), CatWISE2020, AllWISE, unWISE and 2MASS (NOIRLab Astro Data Lab), UltracoolSheet labels. Model: Python, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, Astropy and scikit-learn gradient boosting, trained in about one hour on a personal computer. Viewer: [frontend framework], deployed on Vercel. Git for version control. AI assistants (Claude and ChatGPT) helped write and audit code and documentation.

Creativity. We turn images whose wavelength changes across the detector into a simple “watch the sky change” experience, and we let two AI systems audit each other, one building and one reviewing, with every objection recorded.

Factors we considered. Objects move between surveys, so positions are propagated to each observation date. Labels are few and partly circular, so results are reported by how each label was obtained. Models can cheat with brightness or sky position, so we validated by sky region, kept a reserved region sealed, and trained the model to survive losing its strongest clue. We state limits openly: Y-dwarf detection is weak and the external test has four objects.
